_meta.note: Peak positions are typical literature ranges (cm-1) compiled from standard FTIR spectroscopy correlation-table references (polymer/materials/biomolecule spectroscopy literature). These are reference/approximate ranges, not certified measurements of a specific sample batch. For publication-grade identification, always cross-check against NIST Chemistry WebBook, SDBS, or a certified reference spectrum. Every entry below carries a 'source' field naming the reference literature its ranges are drawn from -- use it to trace and verify any match.

references.citation: Socrates, G. – Infrared and Raman Characteristic Group Frequencies: Tables and Charts, 3rd ed., Wiley, 2001.
Pavia, D.L.; Lampman, G.M.; Kriz, G.S.; Vyvyan, J.A. – Introduction to Spectroscopy, 5th ed., Cengage Learning, 2015.
Silverstein, R.M.; Webster, F.X.; Kiemle, D.J.; Bryce, D.L. – Spectrometric Identification of Organic Compounds, 8th ed., Wiley, 2014.
Smith, B.C. – Infrared Spectral Interpretation: A Systematic Approach, CRC Press, 1999.
Nakamoto, K. – Infrared and Raman Spectra of Inorganic and Coordination Compounds, Part A, 6th ed., Wiley, 2009.
Coates, J. – Interpretation of Infrared Spectra, A Practical Approach, in Encyclopedia of Analytical Chemistry, Wiley, 2000.
Farmer, V.C. (ed.) – The Infrared Spectra of Minerals, Mineralogical Society Monograph 4, 1974.
NIST Chemistry WebBook, National Institute of Standards and Technology (webbook.nist.gov) – for cross-checking specific compounds.
SDBS – Spectral Database for Organic Compounds, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Japan (sdbs.db.aist.go.jp) – for cross-checking specific compounds.
Cullity, B.D.; Stock, S.R. – Elements of X-Ray Diffraction, 3rd ed., Prentice Hall, 2001.
ICDD Powder Diffraction File (PDF-2 / PDF-4), International Centre for Diffraction Data – the certified reference for definitive phase identification.
Crystallography Open Database (COD), crystallography.net – open-access crystal structure data, for cross-checking unit-cell/d-spacing values.

elements_allotropes.name: Graphite (Carbon, hexagonal allotrope)
elements_allotropes.source: socrates2001, nakamoto2009; solid-state/lattice-vibration IR literature; cross-check: nist

peaks.assignment: Graphite's in-plane sp2 lattice modes are IR-silent by symmetry (centrosymmetric); FTIR features seen in real samples usually indicate oxidation (C-O, C=O) or defects, not pristine graphite itself.

elements_allotropes.name: Elemental Silicon (crystalline)
elements_allotropes.source: socrates2001, nakamoto2009; solid-state/lattice-vibration IR literature; cross-check: nist

peaks.assignment: Crystalline silicon has no first-order IR-active fundamental (centrosymmetric diamond-cubic lattice); a weak multiphonon absorption exists near 600-1500 cm-1 in thick wafers, and any O-H/Si-O bands seen are from native surface oxide, not bulk Si.

elements_allotropes.name: Molybdenum Disulfide (MoS2)
elements_allotropes.source: socrates2001, nakamoto2009; solid-state/lattice-vibration IR literature; cross-check: nist

peaks.assignment: MoS2's characteristic Mo-S lattice/phonon modes fall in the far-IR (below ~470 cm-1), largely outside typical benchtop mid-IR FTIR range; Raman is the standard vibrational technique for this material.
